title: The first screen of an analytics tool
metaTitle: Analytics tool UX: the first screen
excerpt: Open an analytics tool on the one number an operator will cite, with its definition, window, and freshness. One action should change the view. A tour of charts can wait.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree, a quiet place to read one figure.
caption: One desk, one notebook, nothing competing. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on the first screen of an analytics tool?
faqs.answer: One number the operator would act on if it moved, with the unit, the window, a comparison, and a one-line definition. Freshness belongs there too. A zero that is really a missing import should be labeled as missing. The first action is whatever they do when the number looks wrong.

faqs.question: How many charts should the homepage have?
faqs.answer: One headline, and a second figure only if the first cannot be read without it. A grid of twelve equal charts gives the eye no job. Breakdowns by the one dimension this role always asks about can sit just below, as a table they can open, not as a second homepage.

faqs.question: What makes the number trustworthy?
faqs.answer: A definition that matches the export, a source named in words, and a visible mark when history is restated or a source is partial. Sticky filters must show as chips. Copying the number should include the window and the definition, because the figure will be pasted into a note.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An analytics tool ux should open on the one number an operator already trusts, with the definition beside it and one action that changes the view. A tour of charts answers a question they did not bring.

Nielsen Norman Group found that people often leave a web page within 10 to 20 seconds, and that a clear value proposition in those first 10 seconds is what earns a longer stay. On an analytics home, the value proposition is the number. If it is buried under a welcome modal, the operator will export a spreadsheet instead.

## Name the number

Ask which figure, if it moved overnight, would change what the operator does today. That figure is the object. Activation for a product team. Collected revenue for a founder watching the till. Error rate for someone on call. Open tickets, if this tool is how a support lead sees load. Pick one for the first screen of a given role. A role with five "primary" numbers has none.

Show the number large enough to read from a glance, with the unit and the window in the same breath. "$42,180 · last 7 days · paid invoices." Not a sparkline with the label on the other side of the screen. The comparison that matters sits next to it: versus the prior window, or versus the target they set. A comparison without a baseline is decoration.

Under the number, one sentence of definition. "Paid invoices, excluding tax, in the account time zone." Operators lose trust when the homepage number and the finance export disagree by a quiet filter no one wrote down. The definition is how you keep the promise. It can be short. It cannot be a tooltip only a hover reveals, because the person checking from their phone never hovers.

If the number is not ready, say so. "Waiting on yesterday's settlement" is a status. A zero that is really a missing import is a lie, and it will be the screenshot in the next leadership meeting. Freshness is part of the object. A timestamp, in words, belongs on the first screen.

## One action

The action is the thing they do when the number is surprising. Change the window. Break it down by the one dimension they always ask about. Open the rows underneath. Share it with the person who owns the leak. Pick the action that matches the role, and make it the button. Everything else can be a quieter link.

Do not make the first action "take a tour," "connect another source," or "invite your team," unless the tool truly has no number yet. Empty and connected are different screens. A new workspace with no source should say that, name the source, and offer to connect it. A workspace that has been live for a year should never see that empty state again.

Filters that stick from last visit are a kindness only if you show them. "You are looking at the EU shop, last 7 days" prevents a panic about a number that is correct and scoped. Let them clear that scope in one tap. A sticky filter with no chip is how a trusted number becomes a bug report.

Resist a grid of twelve equal charts. The eye cannot tell which one is the job. If a second figure is truly required to interpret the first, place it as a supporting line, smaller, with its own definition. Revenue without refunds, or signups without the count that activated, can be that pair. A third chart is a different page.

## Trust is the product

Operators forgive ugly. They do not forgive a number that moves without a reason. When you restate history, because a late invoice arrived or a tracking bug was fixed, mark the point. "Updated 6 April: includes a backfilled day." A silent rewrite is the fastest way to lose the only asset this screen has.

Show the source in human words. "From the billing database, refreshed 20 minutes ago." If a source is stale or disconnected, the number should wear that warning, not sit calmly beside a green dot in a footer. Partial data needs a sentence. "This excludes the US shop. That connection failed at 4:10 am." A total that omits a region and still looks final will be repeated in a board note.

Rounding should be honest. If you show whole dollars, do not let the exported cents contradict the headline by enough to embarrass the person who read it aloud. State the rounding in the definition line when it matters. For a rate, show the numerator and the denominator somewhere one click away, on this screen if the rate is the headline. A percentage with no count is how a tiny sample becomes a strategy.

Got Next and Leadly are public examples of product interfaces that keep a single job in view. An analytics home can learn from that restraint. The job is one figure a person can defend. Trade Moai shows the value of a layout a person can scan. Steal the scan, not a gallery of widgets.

## What to leave off

A product tour. A changelog modal. A prompt to upgrade that covers the number. Social proof. A chart type switcher as the primary control. Documentation. The settings for the warehouse. The first screen is not the information architecture of your company. It is the answer to "what happened."

Navigation can exist. It should not compete. The number occupies the first viewport on a laptop and on a phone. The operator may scroll for the breakdown. They should not have to scroll to learn what the page thinks the number is.

Personalization is welcome when it remembers the role's number, and dangerous when it silently swaps metrics because a model guessed. If you offer a choice of homepage metric, the choice should be explicit, saved, and labeled. "You pinned failed payments." A tool that rearranges itself every Monday trains people to ignore it.

## The breakdown that earns the second screen

Once the number is trusted, the next question is almost always "which slice moved." Design that path on purpose. One dimension, chosen for the role: plan, country, campaign, product line, owner. A table they can sort. A way to click a row and see the events or invoices underneath, still with the definition in view.

Do not open that path inside a maze of dashboards with names like "v3 final." Names should match the job. "Paid invoices." "Activation, first 14 days." If a saved view exists, show who saved it and what it filters. Orphan dashboards are how two people argue from two numbers that were never the same question.

The rows under a number are also where permission shows up. A regional lead may see their region's figure as the headline, and should not see another region's customers in the drill-down. If a row is locked, say so. Hiding the row with no explanation makes the total look wrong, because the parts will not add up. Prefer a visible line: "Other regions are hidden for your role. They are included in the total."

## Phone, Monday, and the copied number

The first screen will be checked on a phone, in a corridor, before a meeting. The number, the window, and the freshness have to survive that width. A chart that only makes sense on a 1440-pixel canvas is a desktop souvenir. The definition can collapse to two lines. It cannot move to another page.

Assume the number will be copied. Operators paste it into a note, a deck, a chat. Give them a copy action that includes the window and the definition, not the bare digits. "Paid invoices, last 7 days, $42,180, refreshed 8:10 am" travels. "$42,180" does not. If you do nothing else for trust, do this, because the figure will leave your product and have to defend itself.

Monday is the harsh test. The window "last 7 days" means something different on Monday than on Friday, and a weekend of low traffic will look like a crisis if the comparison is unlabeled. Say "versus the prior 7 days" in words. If your business should be compared weekdays to weekdays, make that the default and say so. The first screen is allowed to have an opinion. It is not allowed to have a silent one.

## Review the first minute

Sit with an operator who did not design the tool. Ask them, at ten seconds, what the number is, what window it covers, and what they would do if it looked wrong. If they cannot answer, the screen is still a tour, whatever you called it.

Then break it on purpose. Disconnect a source. Backfill a day. Pin a filter. Each of those should be visible in words on the same screen as the number. A trusted figure with an invisible caveat is not trusted for long.

When the figure itself cannot be shown, because a query failed or a source lied, the screen becomes an error, and the words matter more than the chart that is missing. [Errors in an analytics tool](/blog/errors-in-an-analytics-tool) is the next piece to design, so a broken refresh still tells the operator whether to wait, to reconnect, or to doubt the last good number.

Hanabi designs this kind of first screen in Figma with real figures, not lorem counts, then builds it in Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Tailwind carries the type hierarchy so the number is obviously the number. Motion can mark a refresh. It should not delay the figure. The definition, the window, and the rows belong in PostgreSQL through Prisma, so two people loading the page get the same object.

If your analytics home is still a gallery, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) and notice which screens trust the viewer with one job. Then ask which number your operator would pin, and whether the product lets them.
